subject: business
book: Business Studies Part I (Principles and Functions of Management); Business Studies Part II (Business Finance and Marketing) (NCERT, rationalised)

chapters.title: Part I: Nature and Significance of Management

concepts.text: Management as the process of getting things done effectively and efficiently through others
Effectiveness (achieving goals on time) vs efficiency (doing it at minimum cost); possible combinations
Goal-oriented process, all-pervasive, multidimensional (work, people, operations), continuous, group activity, dynamic function, intangible force
Organisational objectives: survival, profit, growth
Social objectives: benefits for society, employment, environment-friendly methods
Personal objectives: meeting financial, social and higher-level needs of employees
Achieves group goals, increases efficiency, creates dynamic organisation, achieves personal objectives, helps development of society

sections.name: 1.5 Nature of Management: Art, Science or Profession

concepts.text: Management as an art: existence of theoretical knowledge, personalised application, based on practice and creativity
Management as a science: systematised body of knowledge, principles based on experimentation, universal validity (inexact/behavioural science)
Management as a profession: well-defined body of knowledge, restricted entry, professional association, ethical code, service motive; which features management meets
Conclusion: management has characteristics of art and science and some of a profession
Top management: roles and functions (CEO, board, MD) - overall goals and policies
Middle management: interpreting policies, assigning duties, coordinating departments
Supervisory/operational management: overseeing workers, quality, link between management and workforce
Identifying the level of management from a description of duties
Planning, organising, staffing, directing and controlling: meaning of each and their sequence
Meaning of coordination as integrating group efforts towards common goals
Characteristics: integrates group efforts, ensures unity of action, continuous, all-pervasive, responsibility of all managers, deliberate function
Importance: growth in size, functional differentiation, specialisation
Why coordination is called the essence of management (needed at all levels and in all functions)
Case-based: identify feature/objective/level/function of management from a passage
Explain management as art, science and profession; explain importance of coordination
Distinguish effectiveness and efficiency with examples
Meaning of principles as broad, general guidelines for decision making; principles vs techniques vs values
Universal applicability, general guidelines, formed by practice and experimentation, flexible, mainly behavioural, cause-and-effect relationships, contingent
Useful insights, optimum use of resources, scientific decisions, meeting changing environment, fulfilling social responsibility, management training/education/research
F.W. Taylor and the meaning of scientific management
Science, not rule of thumb
Harmony, not discord (mental revolution)
Cooperation, not individualism
Development of each and every person to his/her greatest efficiency and prosperity

Functional foremanship: separation of planning and doing; eight specialists (planning: route clerk, instruction card clerk, time and cost clerk, disciplinarian; production: speed boss, gang boss, repair boss, inspector)
Standardisation and simplification of work
Method study
Motion study
Time study
Fatigue study
Differential piece wage system (worked example comparing wages of efficient and inefficient workers)
Henri Fayol as father of general management
Division of work; authority and responsibility; discipline
Unity of command; unity of direction (and their difference)
Subordination of individual interest to general interest; remuneration of employees
Centralisation and decentralisation; scalar chain and gang plank
Order; equity; stability of personnel
Initiative; esprit de corps
Identifying the principle violated or applied in a case and its consequence
Comparison on perspective, unity of command, applicability, basis of formation, focus, personality and expression
Case-based questions identifying principles/techniques of Fayol and Taylor
Explain nature and significance of principles; distinguish Fayol and Taylor
Business environment as the total of all individuals, institutions and forces outside the firm's control
Totality of external forces, specific and general forces, inter-relatedness, dynamic nature, uncertainty, complexity, relativity

Identify opportunities and first-mover advantage, identify threats and early warning signals, tapping useful resources, coping with rapid changes, assisting planning and policy formulation, improving performance
Economic environment: interest rates, inflation, disposable income, stock market, value of rupee
Social environment: customs, traditions, values, social trends, lifestyle
Technological environment: new products, processes and methods
Political environment: political stability, attitude of government
Legal environment: legislation, court judgements, regulations
Identifying the dimension from a given example
Meaning of demonetisation (withdrawal of Rs 500 and Rs 1000 notes as legal tender, November 2016)

Features: tax administration measure against black money and tax evasion, curbing counterfeit currency/terror financing, push to digital payments and formalisation, channelising savings into formal financial system, creating a less-cash economy
Case-based: identify feature, importance or dimension of environment
Explain features of demonetisation
Note: impact of government policy changes (liberalisation, privatisation, globalisation) is deleted from the CBSE syllabus and excluded
Planning as deciding in advance what to do and how to do it; bridges gap between present and future
Focuses on objectives, primary function, pervasive, continuous, futuristic, involves decision making, mental exercise
Provides direction, reduces risk of uncertainty, reduces overlapping and wasteful activities, promotes innovative ideas, facilitates decision making, establishes standards for controlling
Leads to rigidity, may not work in a dynamic environment, reduces creativity, involves huge costs, time-consuming, does not guarantee success
Steps: setting objectives, developing premises, identifying alternative courses of action, evaluating alternatives, selecting an alternative, implementing the plan, follow-up action
Identifying the step of planning from a case
Single-use vs standing plans and their differences
Objectives as end results
Strategy: comprehensive plan considering environment
Policy: general statements guiding thinking
Procedure: chronological steps
Method: prescribed way a task is performed
Rule: specific statements of what to do/not to do; no discretion
Programme: detailed statement about a project
Budget: plan expressed in numerical terms
Differentiating policy vs procedure, procedure vs method, rule vs policy; identifying the plan type in a case
Case-based: identify type of plan, limitation or step of planning
Explain importance and limitations of planning
Meaning of organising as identifying and grouping work, defining authority and establishing relationships
Steps: identification and division of work, departmentalisation, assignment of duties, establishing reporting relationships
Benefits of specialisation, clarity in working relationships, optimum utilisation of resources, adaptation to change, effective administration, development of personnel, expansion and growth
Meaning of organisation structure; span of management and its effect on levels
Functional structure: meaning, suitability, advantages and disadvantages
Divisional structure: meaning, suitability, advantages and disadvantages
Functional vs divisional structure comparison; drawing organisation charts for each
Formal organisation: meaning, features, advantages and disadvantages
Informal organisation: meaning, features, advantages and disadvantages (grapevine)
Formal vs informal organisation comparison
Meaning of delegation of authority
Elements: authority, responsibility, accountability; which can and cannot be delegated
Importance: effective management, employee development, motivation, facilitation of growth, basis of management hierarchy, better coordination
Meaning of decentralisation; centralisation and decentralisation as a balance
Importance: develops initiative, develops managerial talent, quick decision making, relief to top management, facilitates growth, better control
Delegation vs decentralisation comparison
Case-based: identify step of organising, type of structure or element of delegation
Distinguish formal/informal organisation, delegation/decentralisation
Meaning of staffing as filling and keeping filled positions
Importance: obtaining competent personnel, higher performance, continuous survival and growth, optimum utilisation of human resources, job satisfaction

sections.name: 6.2 Staffing as a Part of Human Resource Management

concepts.text: Meaning of HRM and its specialised activities; evolution from labour/personnel management
Staffing as both a managerial function and a part of HRM; aspects of staffing: recruitment, selection, training
Estimating manpower requirements: workload and workforce analysis
Recruitment, selection, placement and orientation
Training and development, performance appraisal, promotion and career planning, compensation
Meaning of recruitment as searching and stimulating prospective employees
Internal sources: transfers and promotions; merits and limitations

External sources: direct recruitment, casual callers, advertisement, employment exchanges, placement agencies and management consultants, campus recruitment, recommendations, labour contractors, web publishing
Merits and limitations of external sources; choosing a source for a case
Meaning of selection; why it is a negative process
Steps: preliminary screening, selection tests, employment interview, reference and background checks, selection decision, medical examination, job offer, contract of employment
Types of selection tests: intelligence, aptitude, personality, trade, interest tests
Recruitment vs selection comparison
Meaning of training, development and education and their differences
Importance of training to the organisation and to employees
On-the-job methods: apprenticeship programmes, coaching, internship training, job rotation
Off-the-job methods: classroom lectures, films, case study, computer modelling, vestibule training, programmed instruction
Induction training as orientation of new employees
Identifying the training method from a case
Case-based: identify source of recruitment, step of selection or training method
Explain staffing process; distinguish training vs development
Meaning of directing: instructing, guiding, communicating and inspiring people
Characteristics: initiates action, pervasive, continuous, flows from top to bottom
Initiates action, integrates efforts, motivates, facilitates change, brings stability and balance
Maximum individual contribution, harmony of objectives, unity of command, appropriateness of direction technique, managerial communication, use of informal organisation, leadership, follow-through
Meaning of supervision; role/importance of a supervisor (link pin, guide, maintains discipline, feedback, morale)
Meaning of motive, motivation and motivators
Features of motivation: internal feeling, goal-directed, positive or negative, complex process
Motivation process: unsatisfied need, tension, drive, search behaviour, satisfied need, reduction of tension
Importance of motivation
Maslow's need hierarchy: physiological, safety/security, affiliation/social, esteem, self-actualisation; assumptions
Identifying the need level from a case
Financial incentives: pay and allowances, productivity-linked wage incentives, bonus, profit sharing, co-partnership/stock option, retirement benefits, perquisites
Non-financial incentives: status, organisational climate, career advancement, job enrichment, employee recognition, job security, employee participation, employee empowerment
Meaning and features of leadership
Importance of leadership
Leadership styles: autocratic/authoritarian, democratic/participative, laissez-faire/free-rein - features and suitability
Identifying leadership style from a case
Meaning and elements of communication process: sender, message, encoding, media, decoding, receiver, feedback, noise
Importance of communication
Formal communication: vertical (downward/upward) and horizontal; communication networks (single chain, wheel, circular, free flow, inverted V)
Informal communication (grapevine): networks (single strand, gossip, probability, cluster) and its role
Formal vs informal communication
Barriers: semantic barriers (badly expressed message, symbols with different meanings, faulty translations, unclarified assumptions, technical jargon, body language)
Barriers: psychological/emotional (premature evaluation, lack of attention, loss by transmission, distrust)
Barriers: organisational (policy, rules, status, complexity, facilities) and personal (fear of challenge to authority, lack of confidence, unwillingness, lack of incentives)
Measures to improve communication effectiveness
Case-based: identify element of directing, need level, incentive, leadership style or communication barrier
Note: qualities of a good leader are deleted from the CBSE syllabus and excluded
Controlling as ensuring activities happen as planned; backward and forward-looking function
Accomplishing organisational goals, judging accuracy of standards, efficient use of resources, improving employee motivation, ensuring order and discipline, facilitating coordination
Difficulty in setting quantitative standards, little control over external factors, resistance from employees, costly affair
Planning and controlling as inseparable twins; planning is prerequisite for controlling and controlling completes planning
Planning is prescriptive, controlling is evaluative; both looking back and looking forward
Setting performance standards (quantitative and qualitative)
Measurement of actual performance
Comparing actual performance with standards
Analysing deviations: critical point control and management by exception
Taking corrective action (examples of causes and corrective actions)
Identifying the step of controlling from a case
Explain importance and limitations of controlling; explain relationship with planning
Note: techniques of managerial control are deleted from the CBSE syllabus and excluded
Meaning of business finance and financial management
Role of financial management: size and composition of fixed and current assets, amount and proportion of long-term and short-term financing, break-up of long-term financing into debt and equity
Wealth maximisation of shareholders (maximising market price of shares) as the primary objective
Investment decision (capital budgeting): long-term and short-term; factors: cash flows, rate of return, investment criteria
Financing decision: debt vs equity, cost and risk; factors: cost, risk, floatation costs, cash flow position, fixed operating costs, control, state of capital market

Dividend decision: dividend vs retained earnings; factors: earnings, stability of earnings and dividends, growth opportunities, cash flow, shareholder preference, taxation policy, stock market reaction, access to capital market, legal and contractual constraints
Meaning and objectives of financial planning (availability of funds when required, no unnecessary raising of funds)
Importance of financial planning
Meaning of capital structure as mix of debt and equity; optimal capital structure
Financial leverage/trading on equity: debt-equity ratio, effect on EPS
Numerical illustration: EPS under different debt-equity mixes when ROI > cost of debt and when ROI < cost of debt

Factors affecting capital structure: cash flow position, interest coverage ratio, debt service coverage ratio, return on investment, cost of debt, tax rate, cost of equity, floatation costs, risk consideration, flexibility, control, regulatory framework, stock market conditions, capital structure of other companies
Meaning of fixed capital and importance of its management

Factors affecting requirement of fixed capital: nature of business, scale of operations, choice of technique, technology upgradation, growth prospects, diversification, financing alternatives, level of collaboration
Meaning of working capital: gross vs net working capital; operating cycle

Factors affecting working capital: nature of business, scale of operations, business cycle, seasonal factors, production cycle, credit allowed, credit availed, operating efficiency, availability of raw material, growth prospects, level of competition, inflation
Case-based: identify financial decision and its factors; identify factor affecting capital structure/working capital
Numericals/illustrations on trading on equity and EPS
Meaning of financial market as market for creation and exchange of financial assets; allocative function linking savers and investors
Meaning and nature of money market: short-term funds up to one year; participants (RBI, banks, financial institutions, corporates)
Meaning and nature of capital market: medium and long-term funds; participants
Capital market vs money market: participants, instruments, investment outlay, duration, liquidity, safety, expected return
Primary market (new issues market): meaning and features
Secondary market (stock market): meaning and features
Primary vs secondary market comparison
Meaning of stock exchange as per Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act

Functions: economic barometer, pricing of securities, safety of transactions, contributes to economic growth, spreading equity cult, providing scope for speculation, providing liquidity and marketability
Trading and settlement procedure: selecting broker, opening demat and trading account, placing order, executing order, contract note, delivery and payment (T+1 settlement in current practice)
Dematerialisation and depositories (NSDL, CDSL) and depository participants; benefits of demat

sections.name: 10.6 Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI)

concepts.text: Establishment of SEBI (1988, statutory 1992) and reasons for its setting up
Objectives of SEBI: regulate stock exchanges, protect investors, prevent malpractices, fair code of conduct for intermediaries
Functions: protective (insider trading, price rigging, investor education), developmental (training intermediaries, research), regulatory (registration, levy fees, inquiries)
Distinguish money and capital market, primary and secondary market
Case-based: identify SEBI function or stock exchange function
Note: functions and types of financial markets, money market instruments and methods of floatation are deleted per the 2026-27 deleted-syllabus list and excluded
Meaning of market, marketer and marketing; traditional vs modern concept
Features of marketing: needs and wants, creating a market offering, customer value, exchange mechanism
What can be marketed: goods, services, experiences, events, persons, places, properties, organisations, information, ideas

sections.name: 11.2 Marketing Management and Marketing vs Selling

concepts.text: Meaning of marketing management
Marketing vs selling: scope, focus, emphasis, starting/ending point, strategies
Production concept, product concept, selling concept, marketing concept, societal marketing concept - focus, means and ends of each

Gathering and analysing market information, marketing planning, product designing and development, standardisation and grading, packaging and labelling, branding, customer support services, pricing, promotion, physical distribution, transportation, storage/warehousing
Role of marketing in a firm and in the economy (book section)
Meaning of marketing mix and the 4Ps
Meaning of product as a bundle of utilities
Classification of products: consumer products (convenience, shopping, speciality) and industrial products (materials and parts, capital items, supplies and business services)
Branding: meaning of brand, brand name, brand mark, trade mark; advantages to marketers and customers; characteristics of a good brand name
Packaging: levels (primary, secondary, transportation), importance and functions
Labelling: functions of a label (describe, identify, grade, promote, provide legally required information)
Meaning of price and its importance
Factors affecting price determination: product cost, utility and demand, extent of competition, government and legal regulations, pricing objectives, marketing methods used
Meaning; channels of distribution and their functions
Types of channels: direct (zero level) and indirect (one, two, three level)
Factors determining choice of channel: product, company, competitive, market and environmental factors
Components of physical distribution: order processing, transportation, warehousing, inventory control
Meaning of promotion mix and its tools

Advertising: features, merits, limitations; objections to advertising (adds to cost, undermines social values, confuses buyers, encourages sale of inferior products, objectionable ads) and their answers
Personal selling: features, role/importance to business, customers and society
Sales promotion: merits, limitations and activities (rebate, discount, refund, product combination, quantity gift, instant draw, lucky draw, usable benefit, full finance at 0%, sampling, contests)
Public relations: meaning, role and tools
Advertising vs personal selling comparison
Case-based: identify marketing philosophy, product type, function of label, pricing factor, channel or promotion tool

sections.name: 12.1 Concept and Importance of Consumer Protection

concepts.text: Meaning of consumer protection: educating consumers and providing redressal
Importance from consumers' point of view: consumer ignorance, unorganised consumers, widespread exploitation
Importance from business point of view: long-term interest, business uses society's resources, social responsibility, moral justification, government intervention
Scope and objectives of the Act
Meaning of consumer under the Act (goods and services, including online/e-commerce); who is not a consumer
Consumer rights: right to safety, to be informed, to choose, to be heard, to seek redressal, to consumer education

Consumer responsibilities: be aware, buy standardised goods (ISI, Agmark, FPO, Hallmark), learn risks, read labels, assert, be honest, ask for cash memo, file complaint, form associations, respect environment, avoid waste

sections.name: 12.3 Who Can File a Complaint and Against Whom

concepts.text: Who can file: consumer, registered consumer association, central/state government, one or more consumers on behalf of many, legal heir/representative, CCPA
Against whom: seller, manufacturer, dealer, service provider
Three-tier machinery: District, State and National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commissions
Pecuniary jurisdiction of each commission (as stated in the book and as revised by the 2021 jurisdiction rules)
Appeals: District to State, State to National, National to Supreme Court; time limits
Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) and mediation (where covered in book)

Removing defect, replacing product, refunding price, compensation for loss/injury, punitive damages, discontinuing unfair trade practices, withdrawing hazardous goods, corrective advertisement, paying adequate costs

sections.name: 12.6 Consumer Awareness: Role of Consumer Organisations and NGOs

concepts.text: Functions of consumer organisations and NGOs: educating public, publishing periodicals, testing products, encouraging protest, legal assistance, filing complaints, taking initiative in courts
Case-based: identify consumer right/responsibility violated, appropriate commission or remedy
Explain importance of consumer protection; who can file a complaint
